Presentation to Governor-General

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have to announce that, accompanied by members, I attended upon
His Excellency the Governor-General with the Address in Reply agreed to by the House
in reply to the speech at the opening of this Parliament. His Excellency was pleased to
make the following reply:
MR SPEAKER AND MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES:
I receive with much pleasure the Address which has been adopted by the House of
Representatives in reply to my speech at the Opening of the First Session of the Fifty-first
Parliament of New Zealand. I thank you for your assurance that the matters referred to in
my speech will receive your careful consideration.
Jerry Mateparae, Governor-General.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I move, That the reply of
His Excellency the Governor-General be entered in the Journals of the House.
Motion agreed to.
Prime Minister—Staff Members’ Release of SIS Information
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader —Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why did he tell reporters that Cameron Slater’s decision to
make an Official Information Act request for Phil Goff’s SIS briefing in 2011 was
“nothing to do with my office”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because I believe that to be correct.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of the Inspector- General of Intelligence and Security’s
report that found that his office was deeply involved in encouraging Mr Slater to make
that Official Information Act request, does he now accept that his office was involved in
assisting Mr Slater to make that Official Information Act request?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. In fact, the report does not show that my office was
deeply involved. There were a series of claims made and not a single one of them has
stacked up. That is why Phil Goff had to leak the report yesterday, because he knew it
would not stand up on its own merits.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security wrong
when she wrote: “information which his deputy chief of staff received from the NZSIS
was used by Jason Ede, a senior adviser within the Prime Minister’s office, to assist Mr
Slater in making the OIA request.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, the full statement, actually, from the inspector-general
makes it quite clear that inasmuch as there were any discussions, they did not breach
any obligations of confidentiality owed by the New Zealand SIS on the part of the
Prime Minister’s office staff. It is quite contested about what discussions were held
between Mr Ede and, ultimately, Mr Slater. But I make the point that there was a wide
748 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014
range of journalists who asked for exactly the same information. If the thing was
germane to Mr Ede, how come all of the other journalists asked for that information?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just have a bit of assistance from members to my left
with keeping the noise down so that I can hear the content of the answer.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: So to be clear, is the Prime Minister saying that the Inspector-
General of Intelligence and Security got it wrong when she wrote: “information which
his deputy chief of staff received from the NZSIS was used by Jason Ede, a senior
adviser within the Prime Minister’s office, to assist Mr Slater in making the OIA
request.”—was she wrong?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, I would say that it was contested. Secondly, it is quite
clear that what drove the Official Information Act request from a wide range of
people—journalists and Mr Slater—was the public comments made by Mr Goff and the
public comments made by me. If it was solely germane to information from Mr Ede,
how come every other journalist asked for the same information?

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: So is the Prime Minister now saying that he disagrees with the
findings of the Inspector- General of Intelligence and Security that “information which
his deputy chief of staff received from the NZSIS was used by Jason Ede, a senior
adviser within the Prime Minister’s office, to assist Mr Slater in making the OIA
request.”? Is he saying he no longer accepts the inspector-general’s findings?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I did not say that. I am saying that I agree with the
inspector-general when she said that I personally played no involvement other than a
phone call on 22 July, despite all the assertions made by the Opposition members.
Secondly, I agree with the inspector-general when she said that there was no breach of
confidentiality owed to the NZSIS. I agree with the inspector-general when she said that
there was misleading information given to me, and, on that basis, I have accepted the
apology from the SIS.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order. I wish to hear it in silence.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I have now used three supplementary questions trying to get an
answer to this question, and the Prime Minister has answered many other questions —
which were interesting, I give you that —but he has not answered whether he accepts
this finding of the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I offer some assistance to the member. If he simply asks a
concise question I can try to assist to get the answer. If the member looks at the last
question, he will see that he finished with a part of the question that was concise enough
but he had led in with quite a lot of extraneous material at the start of his question. So to
move this matter forward I am going to give the member an additional supplementary
question. I hope he uses it well.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he accept the findings of the Inspector-General of
Intelligence and Security that “information which his deputy chief of staff received from
the NZSIS was used by Jason Ede, a senior adviser within the Prime Minister’s office,
to assist Mr Slater in making the OIA request.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I certainly accept there may well have been a discussion
between Mr Ede and Cameron Slater on this matter. I also accept that it is quite
contested and I also accept that it was not in breach of any obligations on them. Every
single political party in this Parliament has staffers and politicians who talk to the
media. Yesterday Phil Goff was talking to the media about the contents of this report,
despite the fact of there being an embargo.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he now stand by his statement that “the OIA request was
nothing to do with my office”, given that he just said in that answer that he accepted
25 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 749
that Jason Ede and Cameron Slater, when Jason Ede was working in his office,
discussed this very matter?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Absolutely it was nothing to do with my office. If you look at
paragraph 225 of the report it says—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How can you say that?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Oh well, you will not like to hear this because I know that it
bursts your bubble, but here we go. It said: “The inspector did not find any indication of
collusion by or direction to t he New Zealand SIS over the request.” The simple facts of
life are that a wide range of people asked for information. The SIS made a decision how
to process it. The SIS made the decision when it was released. It was nothing to do with
my office and nothing to do with me. That is the problem is it not?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I have called Dr Russel Norman for a
supplementary question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that in his earlier answers he conceded that Jason Ede
and Cameron Slater did discuss this issue, when did he become aware that Jason Ede
and Cameron Slater were discussing the issue of the release of the Goff briefing?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The first I would have been aware of it was when there was an
allegation made in the book and then, ultimately, as a result of this there has obviously
been an inspector’s report. What I have been made aware of is that there was no breach
of any confidentiality or any information, that my office was not involved, and that all
the decisions were made by the SIS. I hate to tell the member that there is a good reason
Phil Goff leaked it. It does not stack up today. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! And I say to the Prime Minister that
when I am on my feet calling for order it is no excuse for the Prime Minister to interject.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will the Prime Minister stand aside from his job as Prime
Minister while a full royal commission can look into the truth around the dirty politics
that he has operated out of the office of the Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, but I will be interested in reading the police report of how
Nicky Hager got stolen emails.
Economic Growth—Reports and Forecasts
2. ANDREW BAYLY (National —Hunua) to the Minister of Finance : What
reports has he received confirming the economy is continuing to grow and that this
growth is supporting more jobs and higher incomes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: A number of reports show that New
Zealand’s solid economic growth is supporting more jobs and higher incomes. Statistics
New Zealand’s latest GDP data confirmed that the economy grew by 3.9 percent in the
12 months to June, the highest growth rate in 10 years, and a tribute to the extraordinary
efforts of millions of New Zealanders in their homes and their workplaces. The latest
household labour force survey confirmed that the unemployment rate fell to 5.4 percent
in September —the lowest rate since March 2009 —and an extra 72,000 jobs were
created over the past year. In terms of higher incomes, the benchmark used by
successive Governments over the years for setting New Zealand superannuation —that
is, average hourly earnings —increased by 2.3 percent in the year, compared with
inflation of 1 percent. So there are more jobs and real increases in incomes.

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: What other economic indicators show that the growing economy is
helping New Zealand families and households to get ahead under their own steam?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: At any given time there are economic indicators that
illustrate the challenges for New Zealand —say, for instance, falling dairy prices —and
there are others that are positive for families and households. Low global inflation, a
strong Kiwi dollar, and more jobs mean that we are not seeing the kinds of inflation
750 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014
increases that usually come with this kind of economic growth. So New Zealanders
have slightly more spending power, as, on average, their incomes are rising a bit faster
than the cost of living.

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: What global and domestic risks does the Minister see for the New
Zealand economy over the next 1 or 2 years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We have some confidence that New Zealand will perform
solidly over the next few years and deliver moderate increases in incomes for New
Zealand households, but it is clear that there are some global risks. For instance, Europe
and Japan appear to be headed for recession. There is some uncertainty about the
Chinese and Australian economies, and some of those changes are having an impact on
New Zealand. We have seen falls in global commodity prices such as forestry and dairy,
which can have a negative impact on the economy. We have also seen falls in the price
of oil, which will have a positive impact, particularly for households, at the petrol
pump. However, we believe that the New Zealand economy is sufficiently resilient to
handle these global challenges.

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: What are the implications for Government revenue of the lower
growth in the nominal or dollar value of New Zealand’s economic output?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The lower nominal growth that comes from, particularly in
this current year, a drop in our terms of trade will affect farm and company incomes,
and also some wages. We expect that this is likely to flow through to the Government’s
books in smaller than forecast increases in revenue. This reinforces the need for the
Government to continue to control its spending and to focus on returning to surplus next
year. We are also focused on reducing net debt to below 20 percent of GDP by 2020 .
Treasury will include its best assessment of these circumstances in the half-year update
next month. This is an unusual combination of economic circumstances, but we believe
that the strength of the economy and constrained Government spending can deliver a
surplus when the final accounts are published around this time next year.
Prime Minister—Staff Members’ Release of SIS Information
3. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement regarding the release of NZSIS documents to Cameron Slater that
“The basic claim that somehow my office was either pressuring the system, speeding up
the process, injecting itself in the process, all of that is flatly incorrect, the inspector
when she goes and does her work and looks at it, will, I’m totally confident,
demonstrate that”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, let me start by congratulating the
Leader of the Opposition. Secondly, the answer to that question is yes, and I quote
directly from the report, where it says: “The decision to release redacted copies of the
meeting documents, the timing of the release and the decision to release information
solely to Mr Slater were all made by NZSIS.”, without my office’s involvement.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How does he reconcile that answer with the passage in paragraph
213 of the inspector- general’s report, which states: “I did, however, find that Mr Ede
had provided the details of the relevant documents to Mr Slater and was in fact speaking
to Mr Slater by phone at the exact time that Mr Slater submitted his OIA request.”,
showing his office was instrumental in the politicisation of information from the New
Zealand SIS?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, far from it. There is obviously no doubt that Mr Ede had
a discussion with Mr Slater, but, as I said, the fact that there was an Official Information
Act request was not unique to Cameron Slater. It was put in by a wide range of other
media outlets. The problem was that they asked them as media queries and not as
Official Information Act requests, and therefore the New Zealand SIS treated them in a
25 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 751
different way. That information was all in the public domain because of the stupid
comments made by a number of people.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he now accept, in light of the first answer he has given to my
question, that denying that his office “injected itself in the process” is now
demonstrably incorrect?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No—quite the contrary. If the member reads the report and
looks at paragraph 225, he will see that it quite clearly says that the inspector-general
did not find any indication of collusion or direction to the New Zealand SIS over the
request. Unfortunately for the Leader of the Opposition, this report does not stack up,
and that is why his so-called mate leaked the report—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! That is not going to help the order of
this House. [ Interruption] Order! The number of interjections coming from this side of
the House, particularly from one very, very senior Minister, is unacceptable.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: When he made a political staffer the main point of contact for the
SIS in his office and assigned a subordinate staffer to work with bloggers, what
measures, if any, did he take to stop security agency information from being used for
political purposes?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, firstly, they were not used for political purposes. That is
actually quite clear. That is quite clear, and that is actually what the report finds. You
see, that is the problem. That is why your mate Phil had to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Is that an appropriate form of address for another member?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No it is —[Interruption] Order! It is not appropriate for that
address, coming from the Prime Minister, and I do not want his answers to continue
concluding with those sorts of remarks directed at the Hon Phil Goff.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Given his personal apology to Cameron Slater for breaching his
privacy, will he now apologise to Phil Goff for the partisan political attack launched by
his office and his department via the Whale Oil blog; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The really interesting question here is whether Mr Goff owes
me an apology. He made a series of statements prior to the election, all of which were
demonstrably wrong, and they do not stack up in the report. And Phil Goff is laughing.
He is laughing because (a) he is embarrassed and (b) he knocked you, Mr Leader of the
Opposition, off the news. On the day you were releasing your line-up—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not going to help.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have a point of order from the Rt Hon Winston Peters.
[Interruption] Order! Before the member starts, he will resume his seat. I have a point
of order from the Rt Hon Winston Peters, and I will hear it in silence. If there is an
interjection from any member, that member will be leaving the Chamber.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Pet ers
items.text: Mr Speaker, you told the Prime Minister that you did not
want to hear him concluding his answers like that, and you referred to what he was
doing that offended the House or you. He went on to the next answer and did the same
thing again. What strictures are you going to apply against him?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, the latter part of the Prime Minister’s answer was not
the same as the tone of his earlier address, whereby there was an absolute accusation
that a particular member had leaked a report. That was the part that I was finding
unsatisfactory, because there is no proof of that. That was not then mentioned by the
Prime Minister in the last answer. [ Interruption] Order! Having told the House that I do
not want interjections during a point of order, I do not expect an interjection from a
senior member, Winston Peters, after I have made a ruling —otherwise, I could deliver
the same treatment.
752 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: When will he apologise to New Zealanders for the political smear
machine run out of his office and for the partisan use of security agencies?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would happily apologise if that is what this report from the
inspector-general demanded. It does not. What is true —what is absolutely true— is that
advisers and politicians talk to the media. If it was solely on this side of the House, fair
enough. But yesterday, on the basis of a report arguing about leaking information, Phil
Goff leaked information—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister will resume his
seat.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: When will the Prime Minister commit to all New Zealanders to lift
his Government out of the sleaze and the sludge and stop the abuse of State power for
political ends?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am very proud of the way this Government operates, and I
am very, very confident that the discussions and briefings that political staffers and
politicians have on this side of the House are absolutely consistent with the other side of
the House. And, by the way, if they are different, here is an interesting point. When I
became Prime Minister, members of the press gallery asked me whether I would be
keeping up with the same level of “briefings” they got from Helen Clark.
Free-trade Agreements—New Zealand - South Korea
4. MARK MITCHELL (National —Rodney) to the Minister of Trade : What
progress has been made on negotiations towards a free-trade agreement with South
Korea?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Excellent progress, and it is further
evidence that this Government is focused on issues that will affect for the better the
long-term social and economic trajectory of our country.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: Who stands to benefit from this agreement once it comes into force?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: There will be a range of our exporters that will achieve both
immediate and, in the long term, very substantial benefits across agriculture, forestry,
and seafood. I would like to particularly focus on our kiwifruit exporters, who will be
relieved in only 6 years’ time of a 45 percent tariff that was driving them out of the
market. It is worth about $20 million to them.
Prime Minister—Staff Members’ Release of SIS Information
5. Hon PHIL GOFF (Labour —Mt Roskill) to the Prime Minister: Does he take
responsibility for his office staff passing on information obtained from the NZSIS to
Cameron Slater in 2011 for political purposes?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I take responsibility for my staff,
although I would note that the inspector-general specifically says in paragraph 17 of her
report that the disclosure of any information did not breach any obligations or
confidentiality. I go back to the point I made earlier. Cameron Slater may well have
asked for an Official Information Act request; so did a whole lot of media at exactly the
same time. The problem was they did not ask for it in the form of an Official
Information Act request.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Is the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security therefore
accurate in stating in her report on page 8, paragraph 17: “The New Zealand
Intelligence Security Service information was disclosed by a member of the staff of the
Prime Minister’s office to Cameron Slater for political purposes.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That is her assessment that there was a discussion, but she
goes on to say that it did not breach any obligations of confidentiality owed to the New
Zealand SIS on the part of the Prime Minister’s office staff. Would t hat be any different
25 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 753
from coming down to this House and releasing documents and file notes from the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade in relation to one of the members of this side of
the House —gone by lunchtime? Does that mean anything to you, Phil —Mr Goff, I
mean—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Prime Minister has answered the question.
[Interruption] Order! I will just wait for a little bit of silence. There is a discussion
across the floor. [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I cannot hear a word you are
saying because the Prime Minister is interjecting, constantly.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I was equally having trouble hearing. That was why I was
trying to get some silence. But I can assure the member that the interjections were not
coming from just my right; they were coming equally from my left.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Does the Prime Minister’s answer to the last question imply that he
feels that the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security was not accurate in stating
explicitly that material from the SIS was transferred by his office staff to Cameron
Slater, and is she wrong in saying that the very moment that Cameron Slater pushed the
button to send the Official Information Act request on the SIS, your staff member and
senior adviser Jason Ede was on the phone to Cameron Slater?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It certainly was not my staff. The Prime Minister can answer
either of those supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I said, I am not questioning that there was a discussion and
I am not questioning that there is a contested view on information. I am sure that is
right. But what is also absolutely clear is that the inspector-general has made it clear that
any discussions and any information, if it was exchanged, did not breach any
obligations of confidentiality. They are quite free to do that. What is a breach of
confidentiality is when someone goes to the media a day before a report is due to be
released, because it is embargoed—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Prime Minister will resume his seat. [ Interruption]
Order! I would be very reluctant to ask the Prime Minister not to be here to answer the
rest of question time. [ Interruption] Order! If the House will not settle down, it leaves
me with no choice but to ask members, regardless of their seniority, to leave the
Chamber. The member Phil Goff will ask a supplementary question without
interjection, and there is certainly to be no interjection from my right-hand side.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Why was it appropriate for Jason Ede to pass on information to
Cameron Slater so that he could put in an Official Information Act request for party
political purposes, when the Prime Minister constantly tells this House that he wants
security intelligence matters to be dealt with on a non-partisan basis, when his very
office made the SIS a highly politicised organisation?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, it is quite the contrary. In fact, actually, what the report
absolutely indicates is that there was no indication of collusion or direction by the New
Zealand SIS. It made all of the decisions itself. In fact, all the claims made by Mr Goff
prior to the election do not stack up. So now we have only one question: Mr Goff, will
you deny that you leaked it yesterday?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is not the Prime Minister’s job to be asking supplementary
questions.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: When the Prime Minister has spent 3 years denying that his office
had anything to do with passing information from the SIS to Cameron Slater, did his
staff members Phil de Joux and Jason Ede lie to him about that; if not, why did he
mislead the country?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have not. Mr Slater put in an Official Information Act
request—he is quite free to do that —and so did other members of the media. Unless all
754 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014
of them were on the same conversation, then one has to assume that the reason the
Official Information Act request came in from the media and from, actually, Mr Slater
was as a result of the statements made by Mr Goff and myself —and I am prepared to
accept that both of us relied on misleading information. That is actually why both of us
have got an apology today.
New Zealand - Australia Migration—Job Fairs and Numbers
6. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and

items.speaker: Employment
items.text: How is the Government encouraging more Kiwis to return home, to
provide skills for New Zealand businesses and contribute to economic growth?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): In a number of ways. Over the weekend I attended the first of four job
fairs we are holding in capital cities across Australia. The first job fair, held in Perth,
saw some 1,650 people, the majority of whom were Kiwis, turning up to talk to the 35
employers and business groups represented. The Perth fair, along with one to be held in
Sydney this coming weekend and fairs in Brisbane and Melbourne early next year, are
designed to encourage more Kiwis, and, indeed, more skilled Australians, to move here
to help contribute to our growing New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: What was the feedback from job seekers and employers at the job fair?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: What was evident for those attending the job fair is that
they consider Australia and New Zealand to be a single job market. There was a lot of
interest from people living and working in Perth and Western Australia about the
positive performance of the New Zealand economy, particularly from those who have
been there a number of years. Understandably, some of the desire to return to New
Zealand stems from lifestyle or family reasons, but what is clear is that it is the growth
in the New Zealand economy and its employment rates that are now attracting people
back. I understand that the employers present have brought back a significant number of
CVs and lists of potential employees who will help with the 1,200 or so vacancies
advertised at the fair.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: What recent reports has he seen on migration?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is very interesting, actually. Yesterday the international
travel and migration statistics for October were released. They showed that last month,
for the first time since December 1993, there were more people arriving in New Zealand
from Australia than were moving out to Australia from New Zealand —the first time
since December 1993. It is not a massive number, but it is a significant trend. To put
that in some context, between 2000 and 2005 alone, there were 110,000 net departures
from New Zealand to Australia. So although it is true that there has been an increase in
unemployment in Australia, unemployment in New Zealand is now at its lowest level
since March 2009. The New Zealand economy is growing strongly and more and more
Kiwis want to be part of it here in New Zealand.
Prime Minister—Staff Members’ Release of SIS Information
7. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by his statement in regard to the book Dirty Politics that “They’re based on one
perspective and probably a bit out of context and with a whole bunch of assumptions
that either aren’t correct or are made up, and now can’t be backed up.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. That statement is absolutely correct, as
demonstrated by the fact that the book made the assumption that my office directed the
SIS. It did not. The book made claims about Judith Collins. They were incorrect. The
book made claims about Rodney Hide. They were incorrect. There was a whole wide
25 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 755
range of assumptions made in that book—based on stolen emails—that were just simply
wrong and incorrect.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: In the investigation carried out by the Inspector-General of
Intelligence and Security, did she interview him, as the then Minister in charge of the
NZ Security Intelligence Service and the Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: She did not, and she makes it quite clear in paragraph 222 of
the report that if it had been necessary she would have sought my appearance before the
inquiry. She did not do it because despite all the claims made by Mr Goff —made on
nationwide television and on every radio station that would listen —weeks before an
election in an attempt to skew the scrum, they were all wrong. I was out of the country.
I have not handled an Official Information Act request in the entire time I have been the
Prime Minister. Phil Goff should apologise—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister answered the
question right at the very start.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If one of the central allegations was that the Prime Minister
was aware, why would the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security not actually
ask him that question as to his knowledge?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: She makes it quite clear in the report. She went through all of
the source documents and could see I played absolutely no part—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Apart from the phone calls.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: —other than a phone call on 22 July. That is exactly right, and
I can tell the member about the phone call. In the phone call I said that I saw in the
paper that Mr Goff said he was not briefed. I said to Dr Tucker: “That is surprising
because you told me, Dr Tucker, that, actually, you did brief Mr Goff.” He said: “Yes, I
did brief him.” I said: “I am going on Q+A, I am doing a pre-record in Washington, and
I intend to say that.” He told me that was totally and utterly fine.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If one of the central allegations is not as to the Prime
Minister’s role or part but as to his knowledge, why would she have not asked him
whether he had any knowledge at all —not his role or his part but whether he as Prime
Minister and head of the SIS had knowledge?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I had no knowledge of these matters other than the phone call
I had on 22 July. That is not contested by anyone. The reason the member asks that
question is the same reason that Phil Goff leaked the report—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister will resume his
seat. Supplementary question —[Interruption] Order! This is a conversation you can
have after question time, if you so desire.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why has he argued that his staff were not involved in a
smear campaign, when the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security has confirmed
that they were?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My staff were not involved in a smear campaign. My staff
responded to an Official Information Act request . But here is a very interesting fact: Mr
Goff has now said no one saw a copy of the report, but that does not mean he did not
talk to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister has answered the
question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I want you to clarify your
earlier statement to the Prime Minister about what material he should add at the end of
answers, because he has consistently done it on every single question, in defiance of
your instruction.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept this point. The Prime Minister has continued to add to the
end of his answers comments that will not help the order of the House. I have
756 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014
consistently sat the Prime Minister down. I should not have to do so. The Prime
Minister should accept my ruling and simply answer the questions that are asked.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Did his staff member Jason Ede dictate the Official Information
Act request to Cameron Slater?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have no knowledge of that, but not as far as I can see from
the public statements that Mr Slater made on Radio Live today.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Did he or his chief of staff discuss with Jason Ede the
circumstances that led to the filing of Cameron Slater’s Official Information Act request
in 2011; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Given that Mr de Joux and Mr Ede, of his office, are said
in the report to have “treated information that they were given as available for release
for political purposes unless they had been advised otherwise.”, can he assure this
House that the security services have not been used for political purposes on occasions
other than this?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and they were not on any other occasion either.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Is he expecting the public to believe that his staff got
information seriously damaging to the then Leader of the Opposition, and yet did not
tell him, as their boss?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. Amongst a whole bunch of things, I was on holiday at
the time. It is worth remembering —because all of this is forgotten —that, actually, Mr
Goff made some statements that I believed to be wrong. They were based on the
information given to me by Dr Tucker. I sought to make sure I was right, and then I
corrected those statements on Q+A. That is why a whole bunch of people put in
requests for information. It was nothing to do with, in my opinion, the issue with Jason
Ede particularly. But as the inspector has said, and I go back to this point, insomuch as
there was any discussion between Jason Ede and Cameron Slater, it did not breach any
obligations of confidentiality owed by the New Zealand SIS. The claims made by the
Opposition—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The answer now is quite long enough.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does the Prime Minister not admit that this is rather
strange when it comes to the SIS, of which he was the then Minister responsible, the
Government Communications Security Bureau, which he was at the time responsible
for, or the Helensville raid, when a cast of thousands knew but he did not know, and
that this defence of “I was not told.” is starting to run very, very thin?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member may not like the truth, but that is the truth. I
actually fondly remember being in this House prior to the 2008 election when the Rt
Hon Winston Peters was Minister of Foreign Affairs, and I think he missed Air New
Zealand dropping some people in Afghanistan or something, and “he had not read the
papers”.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is a point of —well, I am certainly hoping that it is a
genuine point of order.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, Mr Speaker, it certainly is, because you have, of
your own volition, got up and asked the Prime Minister to stick to the facts, and he did
not. He ignored you constantly for the whole time. But here is the real point: I want the
Prime Minister to table that, because he is talking drivel.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I accept I am wrong. It was Iraq.
25 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 757
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus
8. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by his statement with regard to the 2014/15 surplus target that
“we will achieve one”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, but we will not know for sure
until the Government’s annu al accounts are published late next year for the actual
outcome for the 2014-15 year. As I said publicly last week, I believe that the strength of
the economy and constrained Government spending can deliver a surplus when those
accounts are published. I would note that that member, Grant Robertson, in his many
spokesman roles over the last 6 years, has opposed every measure the Government has
taken to control spending.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Who is correct: him, who continues to claim a surplus will be
achieved, or the Prime Minister, who now acknowledges that the surplus has
disappeared?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will have to get a bit more familiar with the
facts if he is going to be the finance spokesman. The numbers, of course, will be
discussed at the half-year update. As we have indicated, weakness in international dairy
prices is likely to flow through to Government revenue in the shorter term. We have
confidence we can achieve surplus for the 2014-15 year, but we will not know that for
sure until about October next year.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer, does he agree with his own statement that
lower commodity prices mean the economy will not grow as fast as expected, or does
he agree with the Prime Minister that dairy prices will rebound and “fundamentally the
pathway’s going to be back the other way”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We certainly have confidence in the future track for dairy
prices in New Zealand. I know that the Opposition parties believe that dairy has done
too well. Well, let us try what it is like when the prices are down. Actually, it would be
good if the dairy industry was successful—good for the New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: When the Prime Minister said there were other options to
achieving surplus in the face of a $5 billion hit from lower commodity prices, did he
mean cutting spending; if so, what programmes will be cut to ensure he makes his
meagre surplus?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The economy has a broad base of growth at the moment.
The other options for achieving surplus are simply that the strength of the rest of the
economy—whether it is through high commodity prices for quite a range of New
Zealand products, a burgeoning IT sector, or a big inflow of New Zealanders coming
back from Australia —all of these things will help to offset the impact of lower dairy
prices on the Government’s books. Actually, the growth outlook for New Zealand is
probably improving slightly as we head into a more sustainable economic cycle than we
have had for some time.

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: Has the Minister of Finance seen any reports that it is an unusual
thing to get control of the numbers and to have to understand and digest the numbers,
when you are a person who has twice failed to get the numbers?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That question is certainly out of order, but I will take a
supplementary question from Grant Robertson.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Supplementary question. Here is a number. I have a number for
you, Bill—22. That is the number for you, Bill.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I will now look forward to the supplementary question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of his promise, first made in 2011, of a “meaningful
surplus for 2014-15”, what dollar figure will constitute a meaningful surplus?
758 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: You will have to wait for the out-turn. But what we do know
is that in the Labour caucus one MP who promised Grant Robertson a vote did not
deliver it, and that changed the leadership of the Labour Party. So a small number can
make a big difference.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Out of that highly irrelevant
answer, can I get another supplementary question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member may. The latter part was not helpful for the order of
the House, I accept, but the member—[Interruption] I am on my feet, if the member had
not noticed. He has raised a point of order and said the answer was irrelevant. I think the
answer did address the question. He simply said he is not prepared to put a dollar figure
on it until the December Economic and Fiscal Update is released later.
Transport Infrastructure—Accelerated Regional Roading Package
9. JONATHAN YOUNG (National —New Plymouth)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Transport
items.text: What recent reports has he received on the Government’s Accelerated
Regional Roading Package?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am pleased to inform the
House that work has started on the first project to be delivered by the Government’s
$212 million Accelerated Regional Roading Package. Once finished in the first half of
2015, the $1.2 million of roading improvements at Panakou Hill and Wallace Hill on
State Highway 35, north of Gisborne, will help drivers keep themselves, their
passengers, and fellow road users safe as they travel around their region.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: What commitments has the Government made as part of the
accelerated regional roading package?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Earlier this year the Government announced that it is
investing $212 million from the Future Investment Fund in a package of 14 regionally
important roads and State highway projects. The Government has committed up to $80
million to accelerate five critically important regional roading projects in Northland, the
East Coast, Taranaki, Canterbury, and Otago. These projects are fully investigated and
designed, and address current safety, resilience, and productivity issues. Through the
Government’s Accelerated Regional Roading Package we are ensuring that New
Zealand’s regions, which are a key driver of our economy, have modern transport
infrastructure.
SIS—Confidence
10. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader —Green) to the Minister in charge of the NZ

items.speaker: Security Intelligence Service
items.text: Does he have confidence in the New Zealand Security
Intelligence Service?
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister in charge of the NZ Security
Intelligence Service): Yes.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister consider it appropriate for the SIS director,
Rebecca Kitteridge, to have made public statements in defen ce of the Prime Minister’s
office during an election campaign and prior to the inspector- general’s investigation
into the role of the Prime Minister’s office in releasing SIS information?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: That is a malignant description of what the
director said. The director had made it clear, soon after her appointment, that after a 6-
months settling-in period she would make a number of public statements. That she did.
As I say, the member’s characterisation of what M s Kitteridge did is wrong, and it is
malignant.
25 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 759

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Given that two directors of the SIS have now interfered with a
general election—Dr Tucker in 2011 and Ms Kitteridge  in 2014—why would the New
Zealand public have any confidence that the SIS will use its intended extended powers
in the public interest, as opposed to National’s party political purposes?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: If the previous question was malignant, then
that question was especially malignant. She does no service to her party or this place by
asking filth like that. The director of the SIS is a highly professional woman who is
doing a great job and is acting on the recommendations of the inspector-general in a
very careful and professional manner.
Sexual Offences—Pre-trial and Trial Processes
11. JACQUI DEAN (National —Waitaki) to the Minister of Justice : What steps
has she taken towards improving the trial and pre-trial experience for victims of sexual
violence?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Today I have asked the Law
Commission to resume its work on improving the trial and pre-trial experience for
victims in cases of sexual violence. Victims of sexual violence have already faced a
brutal ordeal, and we need to ensure that the court processes are as supportive of them
as they can be. It is my expectation that this, along with other work the Government has
under way, will make a meaningful contribution to improving the court experience of
victims of sexual offending.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Is she considering as part of this work reversing the burden of proof in
sexual violence cases?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: No, I am not. It is important to strike the right balance between
making the process easier for victims and protecting the right of defendants to face a
fair trial. This Government recognises that the presumption of innocence and the right
to a fair trial are fundamental parts of our criminal justice system protected under the
New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. To my mind, reversing the burden of proof would be a
step too far.
Employment Relations—Compliance with Wages Protection Act
12. IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY (Labour —Palmerston North) to the Minister for

items.speaker: Workplace Relations and Safety
items.text: Is he confident that employers’ obligations under the
Wages Protection Act 1983 are being complied with in light of recent reports of
workers’ pay being docked to recover the cost of theft by customers at service stations
and supermarkets?
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): I am confident that the overwhelming majority of employers are acting
appropriately and within the Wages Protection Act, but I am concerned about the
incidences and reports of deductions for drive-offs at service stations and thefts at
supermarkets. I am advised that it is almost certain to be unlawful. To my mind, it is
absolutely unacceptable.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: What actions has the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment taken to ensure that workers whose pay has been docked illegally recover
their lost wages?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I am advised that in respect of the cases that
have been brought to attention by the media, there is an active investigation under way.
But in general, the labour inspectorate will investigate and require remedies to be made.
What those remedies are may depend on the individual circumstances, but I am satisfied
that the labour inspectorate is taking those matters seriously.
760 Oral Questions 25 Nov 2014

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Given that answer and given that there are just 35 labour
inspectors nationwide, which is one for every 63,000 workers, how can the Government
adequately monitor and enforce workers’ rights against this kind of illegal activity by
rogue employers?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: In Budget 2014 there was a significant increase
in the resource available to the labour inspectorate, and the number of labour inspectors
is now 41. That is a 24 percent increase on the number of labour inspectors who are
employed by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment from the time we
came to office. I am satisfied that there are sufficient resources—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: You don’t care about low-paid workers.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, as to the member who is interjecting, I say
that we certainly care about workers. We certainly would not fire officials for one lapse
of judgment. We certainly believe that a 90-day trial is appropriate, but I would
certainly not support a 365-day trial.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Is the Minister aware of any collective employment
agreements that do not adhere to the Wages Protection Act; if not, what impact will
removing the duty to conclude collective bargaining, removing the right for new
workers to be offered the same terms and conditions as any collective agreement in
place, and blocking workplace access for union representatives have on the number of
employment agreements that do not adhere to the Act?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, no employment agreement should be in
breach of any Act. It is as simple as that. But the member raises questions about
changes to the Employment Relations Act that this Government has made. They are
fair, they are appropriate, and they create a flexible working environment that is good
for both workers and employers.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Does the Minister believe that a worker on a 90-day trial would
be likely to speak up if their employer was acting illegally?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, yes, I would, and I certainly would expect
that person to speak up a lot more readily than somebody who is on a 365-day trial
would.
SIS—Report on Release of Information

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from Dr Russel Norman, the Rt Hon Winston
Peters, and Andrew Little seeking to debate under Standing Order 389 the report of the
Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security into the release of information by the
New Zealand Security Intelligence Service in July and August 2011. This is a particular
case of recent occurrence —the inspector- general’s report was released today— and it
does involve ministerial responsib ility. Dr Norman’s application was received first. I
therefore call on Dr Norman to move that the House take note of an urgent matter of
public importance.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. No one is contesting your decision, of course, but could I ask you what time of
the day you received Dr Norman’s request, because if it was before the report’s release
at 10 a.m.—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has asked a fair question. If he will resume his
seat, I will give him the answer. Dr Norman’s request was received at 6 minutes past 10,
the Rt Hon Winston Peters’ was received at 8 minutes past 10, and Mr Little’s was
received at 8 and a half minutes past 10. I therefore call on Dr Russel Norman.
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 761

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I move, That the House take note of
a matter of urgent public importance . The issue before us today could not be graver.
The issue is that the Prime Minister is using the security services to smear his political
opponents. It could not be a graver issue. We have had to deal with the issue of previous
Ministers who have interfered in police investigations of National Party donors. That
was another occasion on which we had an urgent debate in this House —another terrible
occasion for our democracy. But today—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: —and Steven Joyce laughs about that occasion. On that
occasion it was a Minister of the Crown interfering in a police investigation for a
National Party donor. It was a shocking event. Anyone who knows anything about what
happened will know that it was a shocking event. Maurice Williamson did a terrible
thing. On this occasion we have the Prime Minister’s office using the security services
to smear his political opponents. It is hard, really, to find the words to describe how
damaging this is for our democracy when the Prime Minister himself is using the
security services to smear a political opponent. It is an extremely dark day for our
democracy. It is extremely damaging to our democracy when the Prime Minister uses
the SIS in this manner.
What the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security found was that the Prime
Minister’s former deputy chief of staff Phil de Joux got a briefing from the SIS
regarding Mr Goff. He used that information to talk to Jason Ede, who was also the
Prime Minister’s staffer. Jason Ede then rang up Cameron Slater, who is an attack
blogger and is one of John Key’s friends. That attack blogger, Cameron Slater, then did
an Official Information Act request while he was on the phone to Jason Ede in order t o
get the information. So the Prime Minister’s deputy chief of staff was using information
he received in a security briefing in order to smear Mr Goff, who was at that time the
Leader of the Opposition. That is what the Inspector-General of Intelligence and
Security has found in her report today. It could hardly be more serious for our
democracy when the Prime Minister abuses his access to security information in order
to smear his political opponents, but that is exactly what is in the inspector- general’s
report.
The report vindicates one of the central claims of Nicky Hager’s book Dirty Politics,
which was released during the election campaign. At the time the Prime Minister said
these were baseless allegations. In fact, the inspector-general’s report has found that one
of the central claims in Nicky Hager’s book was true. That was the claim that the Prime
Minister runs a “dark ops” operation— whatever you want to call it —a “dirty politics”
operation out of his office, that is, through Jason Ede and now, it turns out, Phil de Joux
as well, who was the deputy chief of staff of the Prime Minister. They ran that operation
out of the Prime Minister’s office and had no boundaries in their abuse of power in
order to smear their political opponents. On this occasi on what the Prime Minister’s
office did—

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: Say it like you mean it.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Mr English?

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: Say it like you mean it.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: It is true, Mr English, and you know it is true. It is in the
inspector-general’s own report that the Prime Minister’s deputy chief of staff received a
briefing from the security services and told Mr Ede about the briefing. Mr Ede then
contacted Mr Slater, and while they were on the phone Mr Slater put in the Official
Information Act request for the report. Those are the facts in the inspector- general’s
report. And what those facts show is that the Prime Minister of New Zealand is abusing
his power in order to use the security agencies to smear his political opponents. It is an
762 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
extremely dark day in our democracy. The Prime Minister should step aside. There
should be a royal commission of investigation into what is going on inside the Prime
Minister’s office when w e have a Prime Minister who is abusing his access to security
briefings.
Perhaps one of the other really disturbing elements of this is the politicisation of the
SIS. The SIS, in fact, has certain limits in its Act, the New Zealand Security Intelligence
Service Act. It is not supposed to actually support, or get in the way of, political parties.
Yet the verbatim conversations between the director of the SIS, Warren Tucker, and Mr
de Joux, who was the deputy chief of staff, show that Mr Tucker was overtly party
political and was trying to stop members of the Opposition from criticising the SIS and
the Government of the day. Annette King gets a special mention in the report because
she dared to criticise the Government of the day, so Warren Tucker said: “Well,  we
have to try to stop that, don’t we?”.
What we have seen is that the SIS has now intervened in two consecutive elections
on behalf of the National Party. In 2011 Warren Tucker helped the National Party to
attack Phil Goff. In 2014 the new director, Rebecca Kitteridge, amazingly, in the middle
of an election campaign, put out a statement defending the Prime Minister’s handling of
this exact issue—of this exact issue—in which the Prime Minister has been found to be
acting in a way that is undermining our fundamental principles of our democracy. The
Prime Minister used the Security Intelligence Service in order to smear Phil Goff. It was
a shocking—a shocking—abuse of power.
The Prime Minister today in question time bounced around here and there, trying to
avoid responsibility for the actions in his office. The Prime Minister cannot have it both
ways. Either he knew, or had wilful ignorance of, what was going on in his office, or he
did not—he was completely out of control and he did not know what was going on in
his own Prime Minister’s office. It is one or the other. Which is it? Is it that he knew,
and approved of, what Jason Ede and Phil de Joux were doing, which was using the
information from the security services to smear political opponents? Or was he so out of
touch with his office —so out of control of the Prime Minister’s office— that he did not
know what was going on? Phil de Joux, Jason Ede, Cameron Slater—I mean, he just did
not know what was going on.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: He used to phone Cameron Slater.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: That is right. That is right, Mr Parker. He would phone
Cameron Slater. Remember, John Key is at both ends of this. He would phone and talk
to Cameron Slater directly. He did not rely on just Jason Ede to work with Cameron
Slater; he did it himself, directly, in order to help Cameron Slater use security
information to attack Phil Goff, who was Leader of the Opposition. The Prime Minister
of New Zealand was assisting Cameron Slater to help him attack Phil Goff, who was
Leader of the Opposition. The office of the Prime Minister of New Zealand was
accessing information from the security services in order to pass it on to an attack
blogger to attack the Leader of the Opposition. And Warren Tucker, in a disgraceful act,
I mean a truly disgraceful act —the conversation between Warren Tucker and Phil de
Joux, in the inspector-general’s report, is really disgraceful, where it is clear that Warren
Tucker identifies with the Government of the day and is out to help it undermine the
Labour Party. I know that Phil Goff has treated Warren Tucker in a very respectful
manner over many years—I have seen it myself —and I think it is a shameful thing that
Warren Tucker has done and I think what Phil De Joux did is shameful for our
democracy as well.
The Prime Minister says that he did not know anything about this. That is his
essential line. It simply defies belief that in the Prime Minister’s office the deputy chief
of staff was running his own “black ops” operations.  That is what the Prime Minister is
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 763
asking us to believe. He is asking us to believe that the deputy chief of staff —of his
own volition, independently and completely to the ignorance of the Prime Minister —
was working with Jason Ede to contact Cameron Slater to leak information from the
security services to an attack blogger in order to attack the Labour Party. That is what
the Prime Minister is asking us to believe: he had no knowledge of any of this. Jason
Ede broke into the Labour Party database without permission, where there were credit
card records, all range of private records kept —Jason Ede broke in there, but, oh, the
Prime Minister knew nothing of this. The Prime Minister knew nothing of the fact that
his deputy chief of staff, Phil de Joux, was passing on information that he had received
as a briefing from the Security Intelligence Service. The Prime Minister did not know
that his deputy chief of staff was doing this.
That is what the National Party is asking New Zealanders to believe and it is what we
saw from the Prime Minister’s absolutely disgraceful performance in question time
today. He tried to tell us that black is white, war is peace, and ignorance is strength. He
tried to tell us that the inspector- general’s report said no such thing and t hat it did not
implicate his staff, when the inspector- generals’ report is absolutely black and white
that the Prime Minister’s office was completely involved in this and had full knowledge
of what was going on. We saw the Prime Minister’s disgraceful perf ormance where he
tried to say that the inspector-general said that black is white, where he tried to say that
he could not have possibly have known what was going on. The Prime Minister knew.
That is the truth. The despicable truth is that the Prime Minister knew. That is the reality
of this situation.
All of us in New Zealand now have to face this thing. We think ourselves as having
clean, honest politics. Well, we do not. I am sorry, but it is not true. The Prime Minister
knew that his deputy chief of staff was colluding with Cameron Slater to pass on the
security information briefing in order to attack Phil Goff. That is the sad truth. It is a
corruption of our political process. That is the truth. It is a sad day, but it is time that we
faced up to it. John Key is not the smiling nice guy that people like to think he is. John
Key is not the smiling nice guy that he presents to the public. The truth is that he is
operating an attack politics regime using his access to the Security Intelligence Service
to attack the Labour Party. That is the actual truth because it is in the inspector-general’s
report. I would challenge anybody who is watching or listening to this to go and read
the report of the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security, because that is exactly
what it says.
It is a dark day and it is time for John Key, for the good of the country, to step aside.
He is not fit for the job. He is not fit. He does not have the ethical standards. He has the
ethical standards of a junkyard dog. That is the truth of it.

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: Oh, God.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: That is the truth of it and Bill English knows it is true. It is
true, Bill, and you know it. What the Prime Minister has done is unacceptable for our
democracy. The Prime Minister knew what Phil de Joux was doing. He knew what
Jason Ede was doing. He knew what Cameron Slater was doing. They were using
security information to smear the political opposition, and that is wrong in a democracy.
It is wrong of a New Zealand Prime Minister. John Key should step aside. There should
be a royal commission of inquiry into what has been going on on the ninth floor of the
Beehive and in the Prime Minister’s office.
As this has gone on, one of the things that I think is really damaging for our
reputation as a clean politics country has been the Prime Minister’s denials. Nobody is
perfect. The Prime Minister’s comments, where he says that everyone makes
mistakes—OK, everyone makes mistakes, but when you have an inspector-gener al’s
report that comes out and documents the role of the deputy chief of staff of the Prime
764 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
Minister and ministerial staffers in organising this kind of attack politics, it is time for
the Prime Minister to admit that mistakes were made, that he has made mistakes, and
that it was wrong to use security information to attack and smear the political
Opposition. When that does not happen —and what we saw in Parliament today was a
disgraceful episode, when the Prime Minister refused to acknowledge any wrongdoing
whatsoever—then it really corrodes our reputation for honest politics, it corrodes our
reputation for running a clean democracy, and it corrodes the reputation of the National
Party.
It is not like the National Party has always been like this. It has not. Let us remember
it was the National Party that introduced the Official Information Act. Fair enough.
Muldoon did that. I mean, it is worth remembering how far we have come with the
National Party since we had Robert Muldoon. I mean, you know, Robert Muldoon had a
lot of problems —do not get me wrong —but Muldoon introduced the Official
Information Act. John Key is systematically undermining the Official Information Act
by, essentially, blocking all requests for information, except for when it comes from
Cameron Slater, and then he gets it in a matter of days or minutes. So how far has the
National Party come? It was not always like this. There was a time when the National
Party stood for something. There was a time when the National Party could stand up
with integrity and say: “We’ve done some good things for New Zealand. You might not
agree with us all of the time and maybe there are some things you disagree with.”, and
obviously we would have the debate.
But this is of a different order to that. This is an entirely different order. This is a
Prime Minister abusing his office —abusing his access to the Security Intelligence
Service—in order to smear his political opponents. This is a different kind of a thing.
This is almost beyond politics. This is about the kind of country we want to have. The
National Party needs to look at itself in the mirror and say to itself: “Is this really the
kind of party we want to become?”. Mr Speaker, is this really the kind of National Party
that you signed up to?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Is this really the kind of National Party that should be a
responsible Government, about which people can say: “Yes, we might disagree with it
about this or that, but it basically has integrity.”? When t he Prime Minister has denied
all wrongdoing, he has stepped over a line. He has stepped over a line. He should step
down, step aside, and let a royal commission of inquiry look into what he has been
doing. I think that when all is said and done, it will really be up to the National Party
caucus—those who are here in this House today —and others to look at themselves and
ask: “Is this how we want to finish our third term in Parliament, with this kind of cloud
hanging over us?”. It is unacceptable. It needs to  change. The Prime Minister needs to
step aside.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Can I start by utterly refuting the
allegations made by the Greens. I mean, the Greens asked for the inquiry, and now they
are very disappointed that it has not proven their case. The Green Party is a political
movement that was party to the large-scale stealing of emails published in a book 6
weeks before an election—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I take offence at the allegation
that the Green Party was involved in the theft of emails. I seek a withdrawal—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume her seat. We have just had a very
robust cont ribution with a number of allegations from the member’s co -leader. The
Minister has every right to respond.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is it a fresh point of order?
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 765

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I am just—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is it a fresh—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Then I will hear it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it now your ruling that when a member takes offence, you will not
treat that as it has been treated in the past, which is that the integrity of the member
taking offence is considered sacrosanct and a withdrawal and apology is always
required? Are you reversing that many-decades-long ruling?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is not the ruling. If offence is taken and I consider that there is
a reason for offence to be taken, I will immediately ask for that to be responded to. But
in this case, there was a very robust debate. A very robust number of allegations were
made by the previous speaker, Dr Russel Norman, and the Minister has every right to
respond to those. And I did ask the member whether she was raising a fresh point of
order. She has, effectively, relitigated the ruling I have already made.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the public will draw their own conclusions about the
involvement of the Greens prior to the 2014 election; an involvement we are now
grateful for, as it helped to get the Government re-elected because of the excessive
stupidity of the allegations made at the time. I thought that those members would have
learnt.
The fact is that John Key, as Prime Minister, runs the most open, most transparent
Government that New Zealand has seen, and particularly in respect of the intelligence
services. He has taken on the job that others did not take on —that is, of bringing
transparency and thoroughness to the operation of our intelligence services.
[Interruption]
Well, I had some experience of working with the previous Labour Government as
Leader of the Opposition, and I am not going to bother Parliament with some of the
twists and turns of that experience. But what I can tell you now is that Helen Clark
would never have had an inspector-general scrutinise the phone records, emails, and
correspondence of the SIS. That was never ever contemplated. John Key has put that in
place, with the assistance of the Attorney-General, and that is why we have this report
here today. The Greens asked for the report and, because it came to conclusions that did
not suit their conspiracy theory, they now effectively reject the findings of the report.
So let us just see what those findings were that the inspector-general found. The New
Zealand SIS disclosed incomplete, inaccurate, and misleading information to the Prime
Minister and his office, and, in that sense, the same misleading and inaccurate
information was also disclosed under the Official Information Act to the said Cameron
Slater. The information that was disclosed by a member of the staff did not breach any
obligations of confidentiality owed to the New Zealand SIS.
This is the most objectionable part of Russel Norman’s speech: he led this Parliament
to believe that, somehow, people in the Prime Minister’s office used information to
which they had privileged access to smear their political opponents, and that is wrong —
that is wrong. Remember what the information was. Phil Goff, having started all this by
accusing the New Zealand SIS of not doing its job over the Israeli services, said that he
had been briefed by the SIS, and the SIS, for various reasons, believed that he had been
briefed. That was the information—that was the information. The SIS said—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: No, no—precisely—that is what the inspector-general found. It was
the man you said had integrity who lacked professionalism.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the Prime Minister’s office set out to establish whether
the Leader of the Opposition had been briefed, and it was advised by the SIS several
times—from being checked several times —that he had been briefed. The inspector-
general makes it quite clear that that piece of information and the documentation around
766 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
the briefing was suitably declassified. There was no privileged access to the
information.
In fact, Phil Goff had broadcast precisely that piece of information. He had said
publicly: “I was briefed.” It was not a secret. It was not some kind of classified, highly
secret bit of information. The Prime Minister’s office was verifying that information.
That is why Russel Norman’s speech was so wrong. He was trying to conjure up some
kind of Soviet-style system where the secret information held by the SIS was used to
smear people. The inspector- general’s report makes it absolut ely clear that that did not
happen. The Greens should stop misrepresenting the inspector- general’s report. It says
that the Prime Minister’s involvement in the events was limited to a briefing given to
him by the director by phone on 22 July, and media comments by him published on 24
July, 4 August, and 6 August.
This is an inspector-general who had access to every phone call, every document,
every classified item, and it was an investigation into the activities of our intelligence
agencies of a sort that has never been carried out before. That has never happened
before. And despite his having access to every piece of information possible, the
inspector-general came to the conclusion that the Prime Minister was not doing what the
Opposition said he was doing— that is, the Opposition’s allegations were simply wrong
and do not stand up to scrutiny.
The report is pretty tough on the former director of the New Zealand SIS. There is no
doubt about that. He has made a public comment about his regrets for the misjudgments
he made.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Where’s the apology?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the member accuses him of political motivation. What
the inspector-general says is precisely that that was not found —precisely that it was not
found. That will not stop the Labour Party from claiming it is the case —it will not stop
the Labour Party. We know that because it did not stop the Labour Party members
leaking the findings of the report yesterday. It did not stop them doing that.
Let me just read something out. Let me just read out the confidentiality order:
“Pursuant to those provisions, and in order to ensure the integrity of this inquiry, … you
are required until further notice from the inspector-general to keep confidential the
following matters: … Questions … Requests for documents … Information provided to
the witness … Failure to comply with this order is an offence … ”. OK? So when are
they going to own up? When are they going to own up? Oh, so Mr Goff said in the
House today—[Interruption] No, listen to what Mr Goff said in the House today: “No
one has seen a copy of the report.” OK— this is the man who leaked the confidential
notes of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials in 2005 in a discussion with
the Leader of the Opposition. This is a man who was the recipient of large-scale leaks
from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade last year. This is the man who leaked
the findings of this report yesterday, in direct breach of the confidentiality order that he
signed, which states that it is an offence to leak it. So why would the public believe
anything that Labour members say about this report?
This is the confidentiality order, and on the bottom it says: “Received and
acknowledged”. That is, when you give evidence you si gn it to say that you
acknowledge that you are under a confidentiality order and that you acknowledge that it
will be an offence if you breach it. Despite his personally acknowledging that, he leaked
it. And we are meant to believe what the Labour Party says about the conclusions of this
report—the political party that specialises in smears.
Do you know what? It is much worse with its own people than it is with its
opponents. That is why Phil Goff leaked it yesterday —because it was Andrew Little’s
first day. He made a good start as a Leader of the Opposition, and, in fact, it was
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 767
probably worrying Phil Goff about what a good start he had made. So yesterday was the
day that Phil Goff chose to leak, in breach of the law and his personal undertaking, the
findings of this report —first, to spoil Andrew Little’s day, and, secondly, to try to get
his own spin on a report that did not meet his expectations.
The findings of the report are pretty straightforward. The criticism is all aimed at the
SIS. It makes it quite clear that the SIS made all of its decisions by itself, on its own
merits, and, in doing so, made some significant misjudgments. I think that is pretty clear
from the report. This is about events from 3 years ago. Since then, as my colleagues can
explain, the SIS has been going through a significant overhaul, because the way in
which it did handle it did not meet the standards that should be met by the SIS in
pursuing its statutory obligations. That criticism is accepted by the SIS and it is
accepted by the Government.
In the 3 years since then, as I indicated earlier on in my speech, this Prime Minister
has introduced more oversight —considerable oversight —that led to a report this
thorough, which is unprecedented. And, actually, the SIS is going through a significant
review of its own functioning, its own resourcing, so that it can deliver what New
Zealanders expect—that is, protection from some very real threats.
