I do not think there is much doubt about the conclusions of the report. The only
doubt is whether the Labour Party is going to own up to leaking it and whether the
Greens are possibly going to be able to let go of their vindictive hatred of the Prime
Minister. Certainly, nothing in this report backs up their awful allegations.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: What a disappointing
contribution to what is the most serious issue this House will have debated in many,
many years. Russel Norman said that today was a dark day. There has been a darker day
in New Zealand politics. It was 25 July 2011, when the disgraceful, filthy, dirty tactics
of that Government and the Prime Minister’s office came to the fore in the actions that
were about misleading and deceiving the New Zealand public.
Mr English was happy to read from the executive summary of this report. He clearly
has not got into the recommendations. He says that this has nothing to do with politics
and the lack of political neutrality, but that is exactly what it is about. You only have to
look at recommendations Nos 3 and 5, which is that the SIS now has to go and get
advice on how to act politically neutrally. This report highlights just what a disgraceful
level of conduct this Government and the presiding Minister, the Prime Minister, have
over this department. It is shocking.
New Zealanders, many of whom have had great respect for this Government, will
tonight, when they watch the news, be coming to terms with the fact that this is a
Government that does not know the boundaries between politics and political
opportunism and the requirements of keeping a safe, steady hand on the levers of State.
The Government has lost the boundaries. It does not know what the boundaries are.
This report is very clear. If nobody knows what the central failing act was on the part of
the Prime Minister and his staff, let us have a look at the report.
According to paragraph 218 of the report, on 25 July, when the information was
being exchanged —have a look at this. On the same day Mr de Joux, the Prime
Minister’s deputy chief of staff, when he had the information from the SIS: “On the
same day, Mr de Joux provided that information to Mr Ede”— who had no security
clearance and was not entitled to the information —“with a suggestion that it m ight
prompt an OIA request for those documents. Mr Ede then provided that same
information to Mr Slater”. This is John Key’s friend Mr Slater, with whom he is in
regular contact. Mr Ede then “discussed the terms of the OIA request with Mr Slater
and provided Mr Slater with draft blog posts concerning the issue.” It was all run out of
the Prime Minister’s office. All the allegations of Nicky Hager in Dirty Politics  are
768 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
verified and vindicated in the report. The Prime Minister presided over the dirtiest,
filthiest, grubbiest, vilest operation we have ever seen in New Zealand politics today —
and the Deputy Prime Minister sits there and laughs and giggles.
Do you know what was most disappointing about Mr English’s speech? He actually
came up smelling of roses during the election campaign. He was the only National MP
who, when Dirty Politics hit the headlines—when John Key spun out of control, calling
it our left-wing conspiracy—had the integrity and the honesty to say he did not approve
of that conduct. He knew it was happening —he knew it was happening —and he knew
that it had been exposed. He at least had the integrity to say he would not tolerate it.
Today it has changed—today it has changed.
This is a Government that is in a desperate bid to control a reputation now in tatters.
Not content with denying the obvious, not content with defending the indefensible, it
releases more reports. Is Judith Collins off the hook? No, she is not. The Department of
Corrections is an absolute debacle. It released its report, too.
We know it is all wrong, because this is a Government whose reputation is now in
tatters. This is wrong. We know how desperate it is when John Key quotes one passage
from the report but refuses to go to the next paragraph. He quotes the passage that says:
“neither Mr de Joux nor Mr Ede acted inconsistently with any obligation to th e SIS
when Mr Ede disclosed this information to Mr Slater for political purposes after being
told it by Mr de Joux.” Have a look at the next paragraph, Mr Joyce. Have a look at the
next paragraph, because this is what it says: “The events in issue in this inquiry do,
however, demonstrate the lack of any steps by the NZSIS to ensure that its reporting
relationship to the Prime Minister was consistent both with the requirements of security
and with its obligations of political neutrality.” There it is in a nutshell.
The Prime Minister does not care that the departments under his control act with the
absence of political neutrality, because this is a Prime Minister —the most politically
driven and maliciously driven Prime Minister we have had in a generation —desperate
to cling on to power. He runs a smear machine out of his office. It has been going
undercover for 6 years and now it has been exposed. Well, it is all coming to an end.
The circus is over. The circus is leaving town.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Oh, what a load of rubbish.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Mr Joyce knows. He has been a ringmaster. He has been part
of the ring. He knows that it is all wrong, and it points to what we have all known about
this Government: it has no ethics and it has no integrity. That is the shameful conclusion
that thousands of New Zealanders will now draw. The person they look to, the office we
all look to, the Prime Minister’s office— of course there are political elements to it; that
is the nature of politics. But here is our responsibility. When we come to this House as
MPs, whether we sit on this side of the House or that side, whether we are Opposition
members or Government members, whether we are Ministers or just MPs, we have an
obligation to our constitution to uphold and preserve the separation of powers in this
great country of ours, and this Government has lost the plot. This Government cannot
do it.
This Government cannot be trusted to respect the basic principles of our
constitution—that the bureaucracy, the Public Service, has such an important
responsibility to remain neutral, to give free and frank advice, to do its job, to act in the
interests of all New Zealanders, not just the Ministers whom they serve on a time- to-
time basis. This Government does not care about that. This Government has never cared
about constitutional principle. It stands under a cloud of shame. It is a disgrace.
Those members who have integrity —there are some such members opposite —are
now sullied and dirtied by the dreadful, appalling actions of this Prime Minister and
those around him. Well, it is time for that to come to an end. Who on that side is going
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 769
to have the courage to stand up and say to the Prime Minister, John Key: “Enough’s
enough—enough’s enough, Mr Key.”? The peo ple of New Zealand deserve better. The
people of New Zealand deserve a Government driven by ethics and integrity. Who is
going to have the courage?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Got more ethics and integrity than you, any day.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Will it be Dr Nick Smith? He has been kicked out of Cabinet,
put back in, kicked out, put back in. He knows enough about ethics and integrity
because he has breached it enough times. He is the one. He has got experience. He
should step up and s ay: “You know, Mr Key, I’ve been there, where you’ve been. I’ve
acted without integrity, and it’s time to front up to the people of New Zealand.” It is
time to front up and say that New Zealanders deserve a better approach. New
Zealanders deserve a good, honest Government —just like the chocolate bar. We
deserve a good, honest Government, but that is not the Government we have at the
moment. We need a Government that will observe the very basic principles of
constitutional and democratic governance. And now the Government has been exposed.
John Armstrong from the New Zealand Herald had it right when he said today that
this Government has plumbed new depths of arrogance and contempt. And, you know,
it would be very easy for this Government to draw a line under it, simply by having
John Key stand up publicly and say to all New Zealanders: “I got it wrong. I should not
have had a smear machine operating out of my office. I should not have had Jason
Ede”—Jason “Two Doors Down” Ede; two doors down from the Prime Minister’s
office—“operating out of my office, a political operative, the “black -ops” operator. I
should not have allowed Phil de Joux to breach his obligations, his security clearance, to
the Security Intelligence Service and to willy-nilly pass national security information
around.” The Prime Minister should stand up and apologise and he should say to New

items.speaker: Zealand
items.text: “I got it wrong. Please forgive me.” Is he man enough to do it? Is he man
enough to stand up and say: “I got it wrong. Please forgive me.”? He w ill not, because
he has been in denial. Everything he has said today in this Parliament and the handing-
out of the reports of every other disaster this Government has presided over —and it has
been back for only a few weeks and it has had three disasters in 1 day already to have to
account for. Will he be man enough to say it? No, he will not.
This Government is an embarrassment to the New Zealand constitution. This
Government is an embarrassment to the people of New Zealand. We have another 3
years of this to put up with, but I tell the Government this: we are ready to take you on
no matter how dirty, no matter how filthy, no matter how grubby. You are in it now —
your noses are in it. We know what you are like. We know what you are made of. It is
no good—the people of New Zealand want something different and they are going to
get it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: This issue concerns the
functioning of the Prime Minister ’s office and the Prime Minister’s role as the previous
Minister in charge of the NZ Security Intelligence Service. If you go page 7 of the
findings of this report, it says as follows under point 9: “The Prime Minister and Deputy
Prime Minister made public comments in reliance on information provided by the
NZSIS, and that information was at least partially incorrect.” Point 10 says: “The
Director and the NZSIS also failed to provide any clarification or correction once the
effect of these errors became app arent.” Then, if you go to “Political neutrality
findings” on page 8, at No. 17 the Inspector -General of Intelligence and Security says:
“I did find that NZSIS information was disclosed by a member of the staff of the
PMO”—that is the Prime Minister’s offi ce—“to Cameron Slater for political purposes,
but that disclosure did not breach any obligations of confidentiality owed to the NZSIS
on the part of the PMO staff member.”
770 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
If anyone remembers the movie A Few Good Men , they will recall the famous
interview where a character called Kaffee was questioning Colonel Jessup on the stand,
and Jessup says: “You can’t handle the truth!” . Well, actually, we can, and that is what
this debate should be about today. Let us go to this magnificent conversation on page
58. It is Dr Warren Tucker, the former head of the SIS. He quotes Mr Goff: “Can I have
a few days, please, to think about it?”— it is to Phil de Joux that he is saying that.

items.speaker: Tucker
items.text: “I said, ‘Well, I could give you a couple of days’…”. De Joux— who is he? He
is the deputy chief of staff in the Prime Minister’s office. What is he doing having this
conversation? He says: “Look, Warren”—not “Mr Director-General” or anything else—
“I think we should give him some space.” Tucker: “Well, what I said was … ‘I
wouldn’t want to leave it much beyond about close of play Monday, but let’s do that.
I’ll hold it until then.’ So, I’ve agreed to do that, I want to inform you about that.” And
on and on it goes, all the way down.
Then Tucker says, at the very bottom of this transc ript: “Yeah, he will in terms of
overall credibility.”— that is about Goff —“But anyway, I have agreed to hold it till
Monday, and if he still needs another day or two, I will do that, but I don’t want to leave
it … Are you happy with that?”. De Joux: “Yeah,  I am happy with that.” Tucker: “Very
good. Thanks, Phil.”
Then, over the page —this is amazing, actually. It is page 59: “However, the press
release …”—this is under point 198 —“was in large part consistent with the outcome as
understood by Mr Goff”. What it is saying right there is that Mr Goff was telling the
truth. It goes on further, in point 199: “The Deputy Prime Minister,”— Mr English, who
almost lost his voice in shouting denial today —“following the advice provided by the
NZSIS, commented that he tho ught that: ‘the Leader of the Opposition is going too far
in questioning the integrity of a senior and respected civil servant … If you were given
the choice, I think you would take a senior civil servant … a man of integrity, I’d
believe him.’ ” It is all there.
Now you have got the new person involved, the Deputy Director Relationships,
Outputs and Communications for the SIS, and he is having a conversation. This person
is having a conversation with de Joux as well: “… is the PM gonna come out in support
of Warren,”—“gonna”; that is what he said—“or is what Mr English has said [it]?”. De

items.speaker: Joux
items.text: “I understand the PM has done media … he has done TV3 … So yeah, Bill
[English] had done that on the House run. That will be what most media use … And I
would have thought … I had a chat to Warren before and he wants … the word integrity
to be in, and I would thought”— I am reading exactly what they said —“that line …
‘senior civil servant … a man of integrity. I believe him.’” The Deputy Director
Relationships, Outputs and Communications for the SIS says: “… That’s lovely. That’s
really good. OK —that’s great. Thanks.” So who is this man, de Joux? Well, he is the
deputy chief of staff of the Prime Minister’s office, and his wife runs the National Party
electoral campaigns. This has got an acrid stench about it, surely.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: It’s outrageous that somebody should run a campaign!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I know that “Big Ears” will not get it, because this is
about fact. It is not about fiction; it is about fact. If you go to the point quoted on page
66 today by the Prime Minister—who again was shouting in the House—point 222, this
is what this investigator of this matter said: “Had it been necessary, I should also have
sought the Prime Minister’s appearance before the inquiry. However, I have found that
the Prime Minister’s involvement in these particular events was limited to a briefing
given by the Director to the Prime Minister”, etc., etc. Let me ask this question: how  on
earth could she have come to that finding without asking the principal alleger, or the
recipient of it —namely, the Prime Minister —whether he was briefed or not? Surely if
this was a thorough investigation, even a constable or a first-line police person on the
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 771
street would ask the question of all parties involved. As a former policeman, Mr Deputy
Speaker, you know full well that this—I apologise for that.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! You are not bringing me into this debate.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I know, but, you know, you cannot argue with
experience. The reality is that any police person or investigator would have asked the

items.speaker: Prime Minister this one question
items.text: “Were you advised or not?”, and the inquirer, Ms
Gwyn, never did.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Why not? That is a very good question, and it
underscores the inference that the security services of this country and certain law
enforcers of this country are politically biased, yet they are sworn to neutrality on these
matters. But the most fundamental thing about this is if I was responding to this inquiry,

items.speaker: I would say
items.text: “Because the Prime Minister at all points in time was the political head of
the SIS.” That is why yo u would ask him. Are there allegations that infer that he knew?
Yes, there have been countless allegations. So why would you not do the most
rudimentary thing? I cannot recall in all my years in Parliament a Prime Minister who
has been wilfully indifferent to events happening in his own office and the ministries,
like the GCSB and the SIS, that he is responsible for.
Or is he just bone idle and does not care? Or, worse still, does he resort to not stating
the facts when they are screaming out there for an answer? I do not know.
What I do know is that the Prime Minister is pushing the bounds of total credibility
to claim he did not know. Why was he not interviewed and asked at least one question:
did he receive information or not, yes or no? Incredibly, he was not even interviewed at
all, presumably because she said: “I have found from other evidence.” Well, how would
that be evidence? That is, did she ask Mr de Joux? Did she ask Mr Ede? Did she ask
Cameron Slater? Whomever she asked, she did not ask them to name the main man, the
Prime Minister, about whom all the allegations are made. So what I want in this urgent
debate is answers to why that question was not put to the Prime Minister and who
played what roles in, effectively, leaking intelligence to the attack blogger Cameron
Slater.
Forget all that—has this got a pattern about it? Remember when it was said that Peter
Dunne, a Minister for the Inland Revenue Department, was a prime leak on an
intelligence and security matter? What did the Prime Minister say? He said: “Look, I
want to believe him, but I really just can’t.” And then there was a second investigation,
into Mr Banks and the police report. The Prime Minister’s response was: “I’m not even
going to read it.” This was a police report that saw this man seriously before the court,
and he is still there now, and yet the Prime Minister did not want to know. On the
Oravida scandal, again he said there was nothing wrong —all above board. But in the
heat of the campaign, down goes Judith. Apparently, now she is exonerated —not on
Oravida but on this other matter. But the Prime Minister still does not know.
Then, of course, you have got the one that is paramount of all. Everybody was
involved—the police, the SIS, the Government Communications Security Bureau, the
international agencies, and America’s security agencies. The Prime Minister’s office
knew about this raid coming up, and so did the Attorney-General. He was a prime
informant all the way along and far further back than anybody, including him, has ever
been prepared to admit. It will get out. He can smile, but we do now know of meetings
that he had, planes that were commissioned out of the United States particularly to see,
of all people, him—him. When it gets out, he will not look so flash then.
My real point is that in all of these things, what was the Prime Minister’s offence?
[Interruption] I beg your pardon?
772 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Been at the Green Parrot this morning, have we?
You’re more incoherent.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, how could you possibly go to the Green Parrot
this morning when it is not open? You see, that is the kind of information source that he
has built his hitherto very strained political career on.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have to say that
the quality of this urgent debate so far has not actually been that high. It has actually
been, I think, a bit of a testament to the fact that the Opposition has been completely
disappointed by the outcome of this report.
First up, Russel Norman was, I have to say, in fantasyland —he was in absolute
fantasyland. I have read this report, and it bears virtually no relation —no relationship at
all—to what is going on inside Russel’s head. It is a dark, dark place inside Russel
Norman’s head. But, fortunately, out in the real world the report says nothing like what
Russel thinks, and he should go and read it. It is absolute fantasyland from the Greens,
and they wonder why the public does not listen to them. They wonder why the public
does not listen to them. It is because every time they massively overreach—every time.
And then you have Mr Peters and something about a parrot —although I think, to be
fair, that was partly because of Mr Finlayson. Mr Peters is already criticising the
inquiry. So here we are, half an hour into the discussion, and it is the inquiry that is at
fault. He said the inquiry did not ask the right questions —if only it had asked the right
questions. If only the inspector-general had been up to her job, she would have foun d
that, in fact, the Prime Minister was the devil beast. It would have found that the Prime
Minister was the devil beast; but, no. So here we are with a critique of the inspector-
general.
And then we have the Labour Party. It is the first parliamentary day of the new
leadership of the Labour Party. How did the Labour members decide to spend their
time? Well, you would have thought there might be a few issues today at question time,
perhaps, and that they might have some things to discuss —I do not know, maybe the
economy, maybe China, maybe the Korean free-trade agreement, perhaps the United
Nations Security Council, perhaps some other issues that might have been relevant to
New Zealanders. I know this is a reasonably efficient Government, but there must hav e
been something in the last 2 weeks that they could maybe come up with. But, instead,
the new leader of the Labour Party, Andrew Little, “Mr Angry”, decides to spend the
first parliamentary day working out his anger yet again on a rerun of the Dirty Politics
allegations of the election campaign —which were so successful! They were so
successful at the time, and now they are back again. When will they learn?
You would have thought that perhaps with a new leader they might move on to
something else; but, no. As well as “Angry Phil”, we have “Angry Andy” now. They
are prosecuting a report that does not back up what they say —a report that has no
smoking gun of political interference, no unexplained ordinance of political
partisanship. It actually does not stack up with any of the claims. In fact, the report
clearly states: “I did not find any indication of collusion by or direction to NZSIS over
the request.” I note that it goes on to say that the disclosure of information “did not
breach any obligations of confidentiality owed to the NZSIS on the part of that PMO
staff member.” That is it. That is what the inspector -general says. The rest, with respect,
is flannel from the Opposition.
So we move on to another issue that comes out of this inquiry, which is a little ironic:
the handling of the report. So this report was released at 10 a.m. this morning. That is
fair enough, except that a selective view of this report started to appear in the media
yesterday afternoon. How was that? I thought all participants had been subject to a
confidentiality order. In fact, I think they were all told that “You cannot disclose or
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 773
discuss matters raised with you as part of the inquiry. This order is expressed to
continue in effect until advised otherwise. I have now revoked the confidentiality order
from 10 a.m. Tuesday, 25 November.” So who breached that order? Well, it was one
Phil Goff who breached that order.
The inspector-general said at her press conference this morning: “I should note at this
juncture that I am very disappointed that details of the report were disclosed to some
news media yesterday while the report was with affected parties and under embargo.
Those parties were subject to express confidentiality orders made under the Inspector-
General of Intelligence and Secur ity Act.” I continue the quote: “The premature
disclosure of some details was grossly unfair to others. Some of the coverage was not
accurate. For the time being, I want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the
unfairness caused to other affected parties. I will be looking at what steps can be taken,
both in the context of this report and future reports.”
That is the most ironic thing —the most ironic thing. The parliamentarian who
complains that information has been used for political purposes against him has been
found guilty of doing the exact same thing in the release of the report. What a clown —
what a clown. And it was also a political mistake because he did it over the top of the
announcement of his new leader’s new line -up—the beginning and dawning of a new
day, and “Angry Phil” could not wait. He had to get his oar in—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Once or twice you might expect
people to fling a few things across the Chamber. This member has, repeatedly
throughout his speech, been referring to members by other than their actual names,
which is a clear breach of the rules. Once or twice you might kind of think “Oh,
whatever.”, but he has been doing it repeatedly throughout his speech, and there has
been no caution or sanction from you at all.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Speaking to the point of order—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I do not need any advice in respect of this matter. The
debate has been very robust. I take the member’s point that the reference has been
repeated, but there have, as the member has noted himself, been a number of references
by nickname or other superlatives to various members. The points are noted, but the
Hon Steven Joyce will resume his speech.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. That is interesting in itself.
That is ironic. Some would say it smacks of a double standard, but let us be fair: it is not
the first time. We can all recall—I was not even in the House—a time in 2004 when one
parliamentarian used a confidential Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade note. He
released it to make a political point —he released it to make a political point. That was
what he did. And yet apparently, when this Government does not release information to
make a political point, that is somehow bad, and yet for Phil Goff it is OK. That is
actually the issue.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why don’t you concentrate on the report, Steven?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, I will concentrate on it. The allegation from the
Opposition this afternoon was that a political smear machine was operating from the
ninth floor. Well, there was. It was called the Helen Clark Government. Ask Peter
Doone about that, because that is how Labour started: smearing Peter Doone from the
ninth floor. That is a ninth floor smear machine; it is not what we have today —it is not
what we have today.
This Government set up the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security. This
Government acted where no other Government has to create more accountability for the
Security Intelligence Service. This report is clear. The Security Intelligence Service
made many mistakes, and the director of the time made mistakes. They were bad
mistakes, and they should not have been made. The current director of the NZ SIS has
774 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
apologised to Mr Little and Mr Goff, and has apologised to the Prime Minister for the
inaccuracy of the information and the way it was handled. And that is correct, but it is
not correct for the Green Party to make the most outrageous slurs on the Prime Minister
of this country and this House this afternoon when it is not remotely backed up by the
report. The Greens are relying on New Zealanders not reading the report and actually
accepting their ridiculously fabricated view of things. That is appalling —that is what is
appalling.
The appalling behaviour of Phil Goff and the way he has treated this report, in
express contradiction of the instructions from the Inspector-General of the Security
Intelligence Service, shows that the real dirty politician in this is one Phil Goff.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: When John Key is protecting his own
interests, he is not working in the interests of all New Zealanders. When John Key
stands up and defends his own interests and his own political future, he is not standing
up for the interests of New Zealanders or for the democracy that he has pledged to
serve. What he does when he defends himself against these very serious findings by the
Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security is he completely dismisses his role as a
servant of New Zealand’s people— an upholder of the democracy that has been fought
for in this country and by others. What we saw today from John Key and his behaviour
in the House and the disgraceful personal attack by particularly the Minister in charge of
the NZ Security Intelligence Service is that John Key and his people are here to protect
themselves only, and the rest of New Zealand can be damned. He has shown utter
contempt for the security of our national intelligence services, for the parliamentary
democracy, and, again, for the people of New Zealand.
What we really saw today was John Key treating this serious issue of a major abuse
of power—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Why don’t you apologise to Rebecca Kitteridge?

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Here we go. We can hear the Minister in charge of the NZ
Security Intelligence Service, Chris Finlayson, no doubt making more personal attacks,
as is his wont.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Did you hear what you said today, you disgusting
creature?

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Mr John Key has shown today that he—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise for interrupting
the member. I just want to say to the honourable Minister Chris Finlayson that anything
that I said today was not disgusting, and I think that he should, if he is going to interject
in that manner, make sure that he follows the rules of the House.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: John Key has shown today that he treats this place and the
public service role that he has as some kind of game where you score points for being
the trickiest—not for being the most ethical, not for upholding high standards, but for
being tricky.
Well, let me say very clearly that our democracy is not a game. We are not here just
to win at any cost. This is about serving the New Zealand public, not mocking them. It
is not OK under any circumstances for John Key, or any Prime Minister, to run a
“black-ops” scheme from the ninth floor of the Beehive, no matter how tricky he thinks
he is or how much he tries to bat off questions in the House. The public of New Zealand
deserves significantly better than that. They deserve answers, not sleights of hand, and a
Prime Minister who upholds the integrity and the ethical standards that New Zealanders
expect from that office.
For all the dispute around the findings of the inspector- general’s report, what is very
clear from the report is that John Key’s office was engaged in a deliberate smear
campaign and it would use political information provided to it from Government
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 775
agencies as critical to New Zealand’s security as the SIS for party political purposes in
an election campaign. Steven Joyce tried to stand up and do this, and so did Bill
English. No doubt others will as we go on. You simply cannot stand here in this
Parliament and tell New Zealanders that that is ethical behaviour by John Key and his
office. He did know. He employed Jason Ede precisely for that purpose —to run smear
campaigns out of the ninth floor of the Beehive. John Key allowed Jason Ede to use
secret email and phone accounts to dig dirt on political opponents and to attack them
during the election campaign. Not only that but he used information that was received
by John Key and by his office through the SIS. The adviser then destroyed those
records. The adviser destroyed those records. It is set out in the report. John Key says
that is OK. He is quite relaxed about that behaviour of his own staff and his own office.
The Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security found that staffers in John Key’s
office were using SIS information for political purposes. John Key thinks that that is
perfectly fine and that that is a fine ethical standard for him to maintain. The inspector-
general found that Jason Ede used SIS information to tell Cameron Slater what to ask
for in an Official Information Act request; that Slater and Ede were on the phone
together when the Official Information Act request was written; and that Ede had even
drafted up a blog for Cameron Slater about the Official Information Act request. So the
Prime Minister employed Jason Ede to write blogs for Cameron Slater. That is the level
of disgraceful standard that the Prime Minister allows and accepts in his office. The
people of New Zealand paid Jason Ede’s wages to write draft blogs for Cameron Slater,
to dig dirt on political opponents, and to misuse information provided by Government
agencies to the Prime Minister for party political purposes in an election campaign.
John Key says that that is OK. For John Key, that is a fine ethical standard to maintain
in his office. So despite the desperate spin that we are going to hear from National—and
the members are trying all sorts of distraction techniques today, and we will hear more,
probably, over the next few days. We heard some of the faux outrage today, as well,
from National members.
The inspector-general confirms a serious abuse of power by this Government, by
John Key, and by his office. The report vindicated Nicky Hager and his most serious
allegations in the Dirty Politics book. During the recent campaign, John Key said that
the events that were outlined in the book were “baseless allegations”— he used that
quite often —but the inspector- general’s report shows that the Prim e Minister was
wrong to say that they were baseless allegations, and confirms that the most serious
allegation in the book is actually true. Yes, John Key operated a “black -ops” out of his
office. His own staff were involved in that. He gave approval for that. There is no way
that those people could have operated like that in his office if he did not approve of
those actions.
This is a huge abuse of power. It is not a political game. It is an abuse of the most
powerful office in the country. It was first uncovered by Nicky Hager in his book and
has now been confirmed by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security.
John Key is denying it. We all expected that he would, and that he would bluster, as
we saw in his behaviour today. He has not treated the issue with any degree of
seriousness. He has not addressed the public on the core issues, about the ethical
standards and the integrity that he expects out of his office. He said, instead, that it is
contestable that his deputy chief of staff got an SIS briefing on 25 July, and that it is
contestable that the information was passed on to Jason Ede, who then talked to
Cameron Slater to write an Official Information Act request. The Prime Minister is now
saying that the findings of the inspector-general in her report are contestable —the
findings of fact that she made.
776 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
Her findings were based on interviews with the Prime Minister’s former deputy chief
of staff, who is quoted in the report as saying that he wished that Ede had given the
information to a real jo urnalist and not to Cameron Slater. Slater’s and Ede’s phone
records were used to determine the facts of these matters, and John Key yet again says
that this information is contestable.
It is absolutely a game spin that John Key is playing. He is not being honest with the
public of New Zealand or treating them with the respect that they deserve. This is an
issue that deserves a direct and sincere communication from the Prime Minister, not the
spin and game-playing that we are seeing today and will no doubt continue to see.
It also raises concerns about whether this culture of grime that is coming from the
Prime Minister’s office is bleeding elsewhere. What we have got now is in two elections
we have had the directors of the SIS interfering in the election campaign —first of all,
Dr Warren Tucker with the allegations that have now been proved accurate by the
inspector-general in failing to meet his political neutrality requirements and allowing
information to be used for party political purposes by John Key in an election campaign
in 2011, and then again with Rebecca Kitteridge making statements defending the Prime
Minister’s office when those allegations were raised in Nicky Hager’s book, before the
inspector-general’s findings were completed.
If this is the culture that John Key allows in his office, of practically zero ethical
standards and no integrity, of course it is going to bleed through into some of those
major agencies and the Public Service, if that is how they think they need to deal with
John Key and his people. Of course there will be this interference. We must be
protecting the Public Service from this kind of political grimy culture that is coming out
of the Prime Minister’s office.
We have said over and over that the Prime Minister should step aside while a royal
commission is undertaken into the full allegations. The Prime Minister needs to make a
clear commitment to the public of New Zealand that he takes this seriously, because
time and time again the allegations have been proved true. It is about his integrity, it is
about the ethical standards that he employs, and over and over we are seeing John Key,
the Prime Minister of New Zealand, failing New Zealanders, acting in his own interests,
and, instead, allowing New Zealanders to suffer this continual abuse of power. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: What we have just heard
from the Greens is a totally fictional narrative on the report that has been released today.
It was a total series of smears on upright and honest public servants, and on, frankly, the
most honest Prime Minister we have ever had in this country. I think it is disgusting that
Metiria Turei would get up and smear the reputation of Rebecca Kitteridge, a public
servant who has given great service to successive Governments —served under the
Labour Government as Secretary of the Cabinet, served under this Government, and
continues to serve. I just think, frankly, that it is behaviour that is beneath the dignity of
this House, when the co-leader of the Greens comes in and makes statements like that.
What has been clear in this report is that, actually, there was no political collusion.
All these things that the Greens are alleging did not happen. I will quote directly from
paragraph 17, where the inspector- general says: “I have not found any political
collusion by or direction of the NZSIS in its disclosure of information or any
unauthorised disclosure of information by NZSIS staff, as has been alleged. I did find
that information was disclosed by a member of the staff of the PMO to Cameron Slater,
but that disclosure did not breach any obligations of confidentiality owed to the NZSIS
on the part of that PMO staff member.” So ther e it is—not the greatest day ever for the
SIS. But, actually, to try to smear the reputation of the Prime Minister is completely
beneath what people expect of members of Parliament.
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 777
The one thing, though, that has emerged today —and the member of Parliament has
pretty much admitted it —is that the report, which appeared at 6 o’clock on both
channels last night, was released early by Phil Goff. There is no question about it. He
said in the House today that no one had a copy of the written report, but by doing so he
actually admitted that he had read that report and then he went and leaked it to
Television One and TV3. You would think that surely Phil Goff would not have done
that—surely not. But he is guilty. He has not refuted that claim today. I challenge him to
get up and tell the House that he did not speak to journalists yesterday about this report,
because he knows he did.
Why we know this is actually because Phil Goff has got form in this area. I would
say this is about the fifth incident, at a casual count, of Phil Goff being party to
privileged information that he has then gone and released. You will remember the “gone
by lunchtime” episode. Phil Goff was in there with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and
Trade officials. What did he do? He leaked privileged information. What did we have
more recently? We had a coroner’s report that Phil Goff went and leaked to the media.
It was the report into the death of a soldier in Afghanistan. It was under a suppression
order. The police looked into it. Phil Goff is on a police warning. And now, with this
most serious breach, Phil Goff could actually face a year in prison, and actually I think
that might teach him a thing or two. And then there was the instance where a former
staffer from Phil Goff’s office when he was Leader of the Opposition, went off to work
at the State Services Commission. Suddenly, miraculously, a copy of a Cabinet paper
emerged into Phil Goff’s hands and he was quoting from it in Parliament, but then it
emerged that his own staffer had stolen that paper.
The common thread through this is Phil Goff. This was back in the days when Phil
Goff really cared—back in the days when he was still dyeing his hair, when he was still
doing the John Travolta walk. But now he has given up on it. He has decided that he is
just going to cause mayhem. Last night, on Andrew Little’s biggest day of his
parliamentary career, when he was revealing his line-up, Phil Goff decided that he
would wipe the new leader off the front page and the leading article of the news b y
going and leaking this report. He knew exactly what he was doing. Now he is going to
form the nexus of grumpy former leaders sitting there at about Nos 14, 15, 16, and 17 —
David Cunliffe, David Shearer, Phil Goff —who are going to wreck everything. Phil
Goff has no moral backbone. He knows he has leaked this. He is up next. I challenge
him to get up and say: “I did not speak to a journalist yesterday.” And then I challenge
him to say it outside the House. This is serious for Phil Goff. We are talking a year in
prison for Phil Goff, and, actually, that might not be a bad idea. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I just want to say one thing. When
someone stands up in this House and exposes Don Brash and the National Party as
having lied through their teeth about New Zealand going under the nuclear umbrella
again, my responsibility as a member of Parliament is to expose that lie. I did not leak
it. I stood up in this House, on that side of the House, and condemned the National Party
for its hypocrisy and its lies on that occasion, and I was right.
I want to say that I very much welcome this report. Why do I welcome this report?
Because this report upholds my credibility and integrity against the former Director of
the SIS, Dr Warren Tucker, who was found by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and
Security to have behaved unfairly and unprofessionally, and to have released inaccurate,
incomplete, and misleading information. I accept the apology —the unprecedented
apology—that the SIS gave to me this morning, but I want to know whether one
National member of Parliament in the House today has got the decency to stand up and
apologise for mouthing the untruths that were represented in what the former director of
the SIS said. You have the report; the House has the report. It shows that the director
778 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
lacked integrity —a comment that I never made about him at the time but which is
exposed abundantly in this report. Those members accused me of lying when I was
telling the truth, and not one of them has the decency to stand up in the House today and
apologise for what they did.
The second thing I want to say about this report is that it exposes John Key, as the
Prime Minister, as having misled this country for 3 years by saying that his office had
no involvement with leaking material to Cameron Slater —to Whale Oil. This report
makes it absolutely and explicitly clear. Jonathan Coleman shakes his head and says no.
The inspector-general says that the SIS information was disclosed by a member of the
staff of the Prime Minister’s office to Cameron Slater for political purposes. This is in
the report. I am reading paragraph 17. And then there is paragraph 9, Mr Coleman, if
you want to wait and listen to it. He does not like the truth. It says that the information
received from the SIS was used by Jason Ede, a senior adviser in the Prime Minister’s
office, to assist Mr Slater in making the Official Information Act request. Yet for 3
years John Key has told this country that his office had no involvement in sending that
information to Cameron Slater. I want to know from John Key whether Jason Ede and
Phil de Joux lied to him about that involvement and that is why he misled the country,
or whether it was the Prime Minister himself who was not telling the truth. I think the
country deserves that.
The next debate in this House is the debate to extend the powers of the Security
Intelligence Service. All last week Prime Minister John Key said that this should be
approached on a non-partisan basis. He said that the security and the safety of New
Zealanders should not be politicised, and yet John Key’s office took information
received by Phil de Joux, who got confidential information and was regularly briefed on
confidential information, and used that material to launch a smear campaign on a
political opponent. I say to the Government: for God’s sake, have the decency to own
up, say that you misled the public, apologise for doing it —like the SIS has already
done—and give us an undertaking that this National Government will not continue
through this term in Parliament to use SIS security information to launch smear
campaigns against people. They are smear campaigns, in this instance, that the
inspector-general said have no foundation and said that it was the director of the SIS
who misled, was inaccurate, and was unprofessional.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister in charge of the NZ Security
Intelligence Service) : As the Minister in charge of the NZ Security Intelligence
Service, I acknowledge the report of the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security,
especially her eight recommendations, and I have every confidence that the director,
who I think is a professional and exemplary civil servant, will see that these
recommendations are implemented forthwith. I believe that it is under way already. As

items.speaker: L V Martin used to say
items.text: “It’s the putting right that counts.”
For the benefit of the Greens, I would say that L V Martin was a Wellingtonian who
used to sell washing machines, but they would not know much about those because I
think they prefer to wallow in filth, as illustrated by Ms Turei’s disgraceful question this
afternoon. If she has any decency, she would come back to this House and she would
apologise for the foul attacks that were made on a person who, as I said, is an exemplary
civil servant, and I am sure Labour Party members would acknowledge that she is as I
have described in that way. I do exempt specifically James Shaw from those vicious
criticisms, because I think he is a man of integrity. I say to him that the sooner he is the
leader of the Green Party, the better.
I want to set out what this report actually found, because there were mistakes. They
were serious mistakes and they do need to be addressed. The findings first related to the
release of information: that the SIS disclosed incomplete, inaccurate information, and
25 Nov 2014 Urgent Debates 779
that is not good; that the then director and the SIS itself failed to clarify matters when
they should have; that the SIS was inconsistent in the way it dealt with Official
Information Act requests and that its process for dealing with them was inadequate; and
that documents were, however, released to Mr Slater and others that were not properly
declassified. So that was very important and I do not diminish that these are errors that
need to be addressed, but they are errors none the less.
The second bunch of concerns related to political neutrality findings, and it is very
important to emphasise that the inspector-general found no partisan political motive on
the part of the SIS or its directors—no partisan political motive. But, because of the way
matters were handled, it called into question whether section 4AA of the New Zealand
Security Intelligence Act had, in fact, been complied with. A number of
recommendations that have been made address that issue because it is extremely
important that political neutrality never be questioned. So that is an important matter
and does need to be addressed. It is a duty on the director —not the Minister but the
director—to ensure that he or she consults regularly with the Leader of the Opposition
on these important matters. It is incredibly important that the Leader of the Opposition
has confidence in the director and is able to discuss these issues, because they are issues
that are too big for party politics.
And, thirdly, in relation to propriety, the inspector-general found that the director and
senior staff of the SIS failed to realise the gravity of the situation and the potential for
political exposure, and I think that that was really probably the most serious error. Mr
Tucker, who I am happy to acknowledge in my dealings with him was a good an d
professional man, at least had the guts, as it were, to come out today and say that he had
made mistakes. His successor said we are going to get on to them, and that is as it
should be.
But there have been a number of extraordinary claims today. I do not propose to talk
about the Brothers Grimm fiction that was peddled by Dr Norman today, or the
incoherent contribution, as we expect, from Mr Peters, but I do want to refer to what Mr
Robertson said, because he is a person for whom I have some respect. He said,
hyperbolically, that “John Key and his office have used State intelligence agencies as a
political tool.” That is a very, very serious allegation, but it is not borne out by the
evidence. Indeed, I say to him with the greatest of respect and affection that it was a
sloppy accusation. The report, in fact, said exactly the opposite. As Mr English said, if
poor old Mr Robertson had paid more attention to detail, he would not have gone into
the leadership announcement last week thinking he had Mr Twyford’ s vote and that he
had won it.
So I have emphasised and acknowledged that mistakes were made. They need to be
addressed. But they were not the mistakes as characterised by contributions this
afternoon, and I think it incredibly important that when we are dealing in this area we
address the facts. At the risk of sounding like Thomas Gradgrind—whom I am sure you,
Mr Assistant Speaker, will remember from your days of reading Hard Times —facts
matter, and that is incredibly important.
The other thing I want to talk about is that this is actually a very good day for
democracy because, whether the Government liked it or not, at 10 o’clock this morning
the inspector-general released her report —we had no say over the timing —on the very
day we want to debate the foreign fighters bill. We had no say over the timing or the
content. What has happened as a consequence of the reforms of last year is that the
inspector-general’s office has been greatly strengthened and she has the ability to
proactively commence inquiries, and that is exactly what she did in August this year.
But it is very interesting to go back to 2013, when these reforms were being debated.
Russel Norman claimed in the first reading debate that “the role of the Inspector -
General would not work because sh e would not be an officer of Parliament”. Mr Goff
780 Urgent Debates 25 Nov 2014
addressed me in the Committee stage and said: “So, Attorney -General, you are telling
us to have confidence in an inspector-general who will be appointed almost solely by
the Prime Minister … That is why I say, Attorney-General, that your assurances will not
carry much weight with the people of New Zealand and certainly no weight with the
people on this side of the Chamber.” So they were the comments that were made. The
office was denigrated and the ability of the inspector-general to act independently and
make these sorts of recommendations was questioned, but the fact of the matter is that
that is exactly what she has done. She has acted independently, she has acted strongly,
and she has made a number of serious recommendations. As the Minister responsible
for the agency, I give this House my unequivocal undertaking that I will be very
anxious to see that those recommendations, which are ultimately the responsibility of
the director, will be enforced as soon as possible. So I think it is a very good day for
democracy that we have the inspector-general making those recommendations.
I am concerned about the disrespect that was shown to her and her office by the
person who leaked the report. I say this as Attorn ey-General: I consider that the sorts of
politicians who break the law by leaking documents or breaching suppression orders —
be they National, Labour, or Green —behave in a way that is at the expense of the
system itself. All members have to be ultimately respectful of the system, and it is
certainly not something that one can make a joke of.
Mr Goff made a very important contribution towards the end of his speech. He
rightly said that the Prime Minister had talked about the need for bipartisanship. We
have gone out of our way in relation to the bill that is shortly coming up to ensure —or
do our very best to ensure —that that can be done and I am looking forward to working
with Mr Little and Mrs King and other members of the party on these issues. As I say,
they are too big for partisan debate. I think I said in my Address in Reply debate speech
that at least the two big beasts of politics, the Labour Party and the National Party, have
to have a common view on this stuff. Judging from the contribution —the juvenile and
dreadful contribution —of Ms Turei today, I cannot expect anything better of the
Greens, but I believe that National and Labour can work productively on these matters.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
